title: "Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/24-reproduce/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](24-reproduce-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Can someone else get the same report?

Your supervisor, a lab partner, or you next year should be able to open your
project and get exactly the same report. Today you find out whether that works:
you render the report from a fresh R session, pack the project into a ZIP, and
open it as the receiver would, in a new place.

Use the report from day 23. The examples use the duckweed study
(`duckweed-report.Rmd` and `data/duckweed.csv`; design in
[data/README.md](../data/README.md)): 20 flasks, 10 per group, with F17 spilled
before weighing. For the organic alternative, substitute `organic-study.Rmd` and
`data/organic-recovery.csv` throughout.

**Save today:** the corrected report and its HTML, a tested
`report-share-v2.zip`, `algae-brief.Rmd` with its HTML, and
`reports/reproduction-log.txt`, where you note what you tested and what you found.

## Does the report tell a reader what they need?

Read your report as someone who was not in the room, and use it to find out
whether the nutrient flasks grew more. A reader should be able to find the
question, that each flask is one independent unit, why there are 9 nutrient
values and not 10 (F17), the units, which group is subtracted from which, and
your conclusion. They should also be able to tell SD (spread among flasks) from
the confidence interval (uncertainty in the difference). The numbers to expect:
10 control flasks with mean biomass 32.28 mg and 9 nutrient flasks with 39.63 mg.

Replace any leftover notes such as "insert result here" with your interpretation.

## Does it render from a fresh R session?

Save the `.Rmd`, choose **Session → Restart R**, and click **Knit** without running
anything in the Console first. Restarting empties R's memory, so the report must
now import, calculate and plot everything itself, just as it will on someone
else's computer. If rendering stops, read the first error and the chunk it names,
and fix one thing at a time:

| Error | Usual cause | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `object 'duckweed' not found` | The import was only run in the Console | Put the import in a chunk before it is used |
| `could not find function` | A package was only loaded in the Console | Add its `library()` call to the setup chunk |
| `cannot open file` | A personal path such as `C:/Users/…`, or a missing file | Use `data/duckweed.csv` and keep that file in the project |
| Old text disagrees with new numbers | A result was typed by hand | Check the sentence, or use an inline result |

## Packing the project as a ZIP

A **ZIP** is one file that holds a whole folder, which makes it the simplest way
to hand a project to someone or to submit it. First make the folder complete,
then pack it.

Use the file manager to create `report-share` **outside** your working project,
for example in Documents, and copy in:

```text
report-share/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── duckweed-report.Rmd
├── duckweed-report.html
├── README.txt
├── data/
│   ├── duckweed.csv
│   └── README.md
└── output/
    └── README.txt
```

The `.Rmd` and the CSV are the analysis; the HTML lets someone read the result
without R; `data/README.md` describes the study. Include `output/` if your report
saves a figure there. In `README.txt`, write that the data are simulated, which
file to render, the packages it needs (`readr`, `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `rmarkdown`,
`knitr`), and what one row of the CSV is.

Then, in a **shell**, go to the folder that *contains* `report-share` and pack it:

```bash
zip -r report-share-v1.zip report-share/
unzip -l report-share-v1.zip
```

`-r` packs the folder with everything inside it, and `unzip -l` lists what went
in: check that the `.Rmd`, `data/duckweed.csv` and the README are there. The ZIP
is saved beside `report-share`, not inside it; a ZIP inside the folder it packs
would pack an old copy of itself next time. Give every new ZIP a new name (`-v1`,
`-v2`): re-running `zip` on an existing name updates it and can keep files you
have since deleted.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: Windows with Ubuntu

Copy `report-share` into your Ubuntu workspace with File Explorer before running
`zip`. The Windows and Ubuntu copies are separate and do not update each other,
so after any edit in Windows, copy again before zipping. Copy the finished ZIP
back to a normal Windows folder before the receiver test below, because RStudio
runs in Windows.
:::

## Does it work in a new location?

Listing the ZIP shows names, not whether the report works. Extract it into a
new, empty folder, as the receiver would, and use it to find out whether the
report comes out the same:

```bash
unzip report-share-v1.zip -d receiver-v1
ls receiver-v1
```

`ls` shows only `report-share`: extraction keeps the packed folder, so it adds
one level, and the report is at `receiver-v1/report-share/duckweed-report.Rmd`.
Open `receiver-v1/report-share/introcomputing.Rproj` (the project name in
RStudio's corner tells you which copy you are in), restart R and Knit.

You should see the same counts (10 and 9 flasks), the same means (32.28 and
39.63 mg) and the same conclusion. Point positions in a jittered plot may shift
slightly between computers. If numbers differ, record `sessionInfo()` in your log:
it lists the R and package versions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: the project opens, but the data are missing

Look at the actual extracted folder tree. The `.Rproj` file does not contain any
data, and a shortcut to your original data folder does not travel with the ZIP.
Copy the CSV itself into `report-share/data/` and pack again under a new name.
:::

## Correcting a ZIP you already made

Your receiver test will probably show something to improve, such as a unit
missing from the README. A ZIP is a snapshot of the folder at the moment you made
it, so use this correction to find out what happens to the copies you already have.

1. Edit `README.txt` in your ordinary `report-share` folder, for example by adding
   "Biomass is dry mass in mg per flask."
2. Open `receiver-v1/report-share/README.txt`. It still has the old text, and so
   does `report-share-v1.zip`.
3. Pack again as `report-share-v2.zip`, extract it to `receiver-v2`, and check that
   the new sentence is really there. Add one line to the README saying what
   changed in v2.

A ZIP on the same laptop as the original is a way of **sharing**, not a backup:
if the laptop is lost, both are gone. Put a copy of the finished project on the
supported separate storage as well, and write in your log where it is.

## What does a successful render tell you?

Use two disposable copies of `report-share` to find out which mistakes stop a
report and which do not.

1. In the first copy, rename `data/duckweed.csv` to `duckweed-missing.csv`, restart
   R and Knit. Rendering stops with an error naming the file, because the report
   can no longer find its input. Restore the name and check that the means are
   back to 32.28 and 39.63 mg.
2. In the second copy, replace your sentence about F17 with "All 20 flasks had a
   measured biomass." and Knit. The report renders without complaint, although
   the sentence contradicts the data: only 19 flasks were weighed. (Organic route:
   "The percentage yield shows that the product is pure.")

R can tell you that a file is missing, but not that a sentence is wrong. A report
that renders still needs a reader who checks its claims against the numbers.
Note both cases in your log, and delete the disposable copies so the false
sentence cannot end up in what you share.

## A second report: the algae memo

On day 23 you analysed `data/algae.csv` in `algae-transfer.R`: 24 cultures, 12 per
group, with A19's biomass missing. Turn it into a small report and use the same
steps to find out whether it reproduces.

1. Create `algae-brief.Rmd` at the project root with a short question, the
   import, the group summary, one plot of individual cultures, and a sentence on
   the missing A19. Use inline R for the counts, so they come from the data.
2. Restart R and Knit. You should see 12 reference cultures with mean 28.20 mg and
   11 supplement cultures with mean 33.92 mg.
3. Pack `algae-share` (the `.Rproj`, `algae-brief.Rmd`, its HTML, `data/algae.csv`,
   `data/README.md` and a README) as `algae-share-v1.zip`, extract it into a new
   folder, and Knit there. The counts and means should match step 2. If they do
   not, compare the input and code before suspecting rounding: 33.91818 and 33.92
   are the same mean, 34.32 would be a different one.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why can a report work after "Run All" but fail for someone else?

It may use objects created only in the Console, a personal file path, or files
that are not in the ZIP. Restarting R and rendering in a new folder finds these.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## You fixed the README after making `report-share-v1.zip`. Does v1 contain the fix?

No. A ZIP is a snapshot. Make a newly named ZIP, extract it into a new folder,
and check the fix there.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Is a ZIP on the same disk a backup?

No. If the disk is lost, the ZIP is lost with it. Keep a copy on separate
supported storage.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The report renders in a fresh folder. Is its conclusion therefore correct?

It shows that the saved source and data make the same report on this computer.
Whether the design and conclusion are sound is a separate question for the reader.
:::
